domains.name: Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy
domains.summary: Beyond the basics: migration strategies (the 6 R's), the Cloud Adoption Framework, TCO analysis, landing zones, and phased migration planning. Vendor-neutral study aid. Not affiliated with AWS; this course confers no certification.

scenarios.title: The Six R's
scenarios.situation: A company inventories 300 on-prem apps for migration. The portfolio includes: a stable legacy ERP nobody dares touch, a web app that could use managed database, a duplicate tooling app, and an old reporting server unused for a year.
scenarios.prompt: How should each be dispositioned under the 6 R's?
evidence: Rehost (lift-and-shift): move as-is. Replatform: minor optimizations (e.g., managed DB). Repurchase: move to SaaS. Refactor: re-architect for cloud-native. Retain: keep on-prem (for now). Retire: decommission.
choices: ERP: retain (too risky to move now); web app: replatform onto RDS; duplicate tooling: retire or repurchase as SaaS; unused reporting server: retire.
Rehost everything identically; disposition debates waste time.
Refactor all 300 apps to microservices for maximum cloud benefit.
Retire the ERP since it's old, and rehost the unused reporting server just in case.
scenarios.why: The R's are a triage tool: each app gets the least-disruptive strategy that captures available value — retain what can't move safely, replatform where managed services help, retire what's dead weight. Blanket rehosting imports all on-prem waste; blanket refactoring is a multi-year rewrite disguised as a migration.
scenarios.hint: Which app earns its migration cost, and which earns nothing at all?

scenarios.title: CAF Perspectives
scenarios.situation: A migration steering committee argues over who owns what: the CFO wants business-value tracking, HR worries about skills gaps, and security demands guardrails before any workload moves.
scenarios.prompt: How does the Cloud Adoption Framework assign these concerns?
evidence: Six perspectives: Business (value, outcomes), People (roles, skills, training), Governance (oversight, compliance), Platform (infrastructure, landing zone), Security (controls, identity), Operations (runbooks, monitoring). Each has capability owners.
choices: Business perspective: CFO's value tracking; People perspective: HR's skills plan; Security perspective: guardrails as a prerequisite; Governance ties them together with oversight.
All concerns belong to the Platform perspective since it's all infrastructure anyway.
Security owns everything; other perspectives are optional documentation.
Skip CAF — frameworks slow down migrations that just need engineers.
scenarios.why: CAF's value is making implicit ownership explicit: each perspective names capabilities and owners so value tracking, skills, and guardrails all have a home instead of falling between teams. Collapsing everything into 'infrastructure' is how skills gaps and missing guardrails become migration surprises.
scenarios.hint: If nobody owns the skills gap, when does it get discovered?

scenarios.title: TCO Showdown
scenarios.situation: The CFO compares 3-year on-prem refresh ($2M servers + facilities) against AWS estimates. The AWS estimate only counts EC2 hours and looks dramatically cheaper. The infrastructure team is skeptical.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a fair TCO comparison?
evidence: Total Cost of Ownership: on-prem includes hardware, power, cooling, space, network, staff time, refresh cycles, and downtime risk. Cloud includes compute, storage, transfer, support, and the migration itself. AWS's TCO calculators model both sides; hidden costs on either side invalidate the comparison.
choices: Count everything on both sides: on-prem power/cooling/space/staff/refresh plus cloud data transfer, support, storage growth, and migration cost — then compare over the same horizon with the same assumptions.
Accept the EC2-hours estimate; it's the biggest line item so it's close enough.
Add 50% to the AWS number as a safety margin and call it analysis.
Compare only year-one costs; beyond that both sides are guesses anyway.
scenarios.why: TCO comparisons fail on omitted costs, not on arithmetic: on-prem hides facilities and staff time, cloud hides transfer and growth — and the migration itself is a real cost. Same horizon, same assumptions, all line items, or the 'savings' are fiction either side can manufacture.
scenarios.hint: Which costs disappear from each column when they're inconvenient?

scenarios.title: Landing Zone First
scenarios.situation: A team migrates its first production workload into a single AWS account created with a personal email, no SSO, and the root user doing daily work. The second workload is starting next month.
scenarios.prompt: What should have been built before workload one?
evidence: A landing zone is the pre-configured multi-account foundation: AWS Organizations with OUs (security, infrastructure, workloads), SSO/Identity Center for human access, centralized logging (CloudTrail/Config), SCP guardrails, and network baselines — often via Control Tower.
choices: A landing zone: Organizations with separate accounts per workload/environment, Identity Center SSO (no daily root use), centralized logging, and SCP guardrails — built before the first production workload, not after the fifth.
More EC2 instances; the account structure can be sorted out during the next audit.
One shared admin IAM user per team as a compromise between root and SSO.
Separate VPCs in the same account; accounts are just billing constructs.
scenarios.why: Account structure is the security and blast-radius boundary: retrofitting multi-account, SSO, and centralized logging under live production workloads is surgery, while building it first is setup. Shared credentials and daily root use are the findings auditors write up first.
scenarios.hint: How do you un-share a root credential after a year of daily use?

scenarios.title: Wave Planning
scenarios.situation: With 300 apps to migrate, leadership wants 'everything by Q2.' The discovery data shows deep dependencies: the billing system touches 40 other apps, and nobody knows which servers the warehouse app needs.
scenarios.prompt: How should migration waves be sequenced?
evidence: Application Discovery Service maps dependencies. Migrate in waves: low-risk, low-dependency apps first to build muscle; dependency-heavy core systems later with their dependents grouped; each wave has rollback criteria and a pilot cohort.
choices: Sequence by dependency mapping: pilot wave of simple, low-dependency apps to prove the factory, then waves grouped by dependency clusters (billing with its 40 dependents together), core systems last with explicit rollback criteria.
Migrate alphabetically; fairness demands equal treatment.
Start with the billing system — biggest value first, dependencies can be discovered during cutover.
Move everything in one big-bang weekend; waves just prolong the pain.
scenarios.why: Dependencies dictate order: migrating a system without its dependents (or vice versa) breaks integrations at cutover, while a pilot wave de-risks the process on forgiving workloads. Big-bang migrations concentrate all risk into one unrecoverable weekend; alphabetical order ignores reality entirely.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if billing moves but its 40 dependents don't?

scenarios.title: The Refactor Bet
scenarios.situation: A monolithic order system is proposed for rehosting as-is. An architect argues for re-architecting to microservices on ECS with event-driven order flow — 9 months of work before any migration value.
scenarios.prompt: When does the refactor bet pay off, and what's the safer path?
evidence: Rehost captures migration speed; refactor captures cloud-native value (elasticity, resilience, deployment velocity) at high upfront cost and risk. The strangler fig pattern incrementally replaces monolith pieces behind the same interface, de-risking the rewrite.
choices: Rehost first to capture migration value and learn the platform, then strangler-fig the highest-value seams (order flow) toward events/microservices — refactor where the business case is proven, not as a big-bang prerequisite.
Refactor everything before migrating; a monolith in the cloud is a failure.
Rehost and declare victory; architecture never needs to change again.
Rewrite in a new language simultaneously — if you're refactoring, go all the way.
scenarios.why: The refactor bet pays when specific pain (scaling limits, deploy fear, outage blast radius) has a price tag exceeding the rewrite cost — which is rarely 'the whole monolith on day one.' Strangler-fig sequencing earns migration value immediately while retiring the riskiest seams first; big-bang rewrites combine migration risk with rewrite risk.
scenarios.hint: What exactly is painful about the monolith today — and what would fix only that?

lessons.title: Cloud Practitioner Plus: Migration & Strategy — Core concepts
concepts: Disposition the portfolio with the 6 R's — rehost, replatform, repurchase, refactor, retain, retire — choosing the least-disruptive strategy that captures real value per application. Blanket strategies (all-rehost, all-rewrite) are how migrations fail.

Use the Cloud Adoption Framework to assign ownership: Business (value), People (skills), Governance (oversight), Platform (landing zone), Security (controls), Operations (runbooks). Migrations stall on the non-technical perspectives more often than the technical ones.

Build the landing zone before the first workload: Organizations with OUs, separate accounts per environment/workload, Identity Center SSO, centralized CloudTrail/Config logging, and SCP guardrails. Retrofitting foundations under live workloads is surgery.

Compare TCO honestly: all on-prem costs (hardware, power, cooling, space, staff, refresh, downtime) against all cloud costs (compute, storage, transfer, support, growth, migration) over the same horizon. Omitted line items are how both sides lie with numbers.

Migrate in dependency-ordered waves: discover with Application Discovery Service, pilot on simple apps, group dependents with their dependencies, and put core systems last with rollback criteria. Then optimize — refactor the seams where the business case is proven, strangler-fig style.

example.code:
aws organizations list-roots --query 'Roots[*].Id'
aws organizations list-organizational-units-for-parent --parent-id r-xxxx \
  --query 'OrganizationalUnits[*].Name'
example.walkthrough: Listing the organization root and OUs shows the account structure behind the landing zone — workloads isolated by account, guardrails attached at the OU level. If every workload lives in one flat account, the foundation was skipped.

pitfalls: Common trap: migrating before the landing zone exists — every workload then inherits missing SSO, logging, and guardrails.
Common trap: TCO comparisons that omit data transfer, staff time, or the migration itself — the side with more hidden costs always 'wins.'
Common trap: big-bang cutovers for dependency-heavy systems — one failed cutover rolls back everything at once.
Common trap: refactoring as a migration prerequisite — combine rewrite risk with migration risk and both slip; rehost, then strangler-fig.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Disposition a Mini Portfolio
labs.objective: Apply the 6 R's to a sample application portfolio and defend each choice.
steps: List 6 fictional apps with one-line descriptions (legacy ERP, marketing site, duplicate wiki, dev sandbox, email system, unused reporting DB).
Assign one R to each with a one-sentence justification tied to value vs effort.
Identify which two you'd migrate in the pilot wave and why.
Note which disposition you'd revisit in 12 months (retain/revisit candidates).

labs.title: Sketch the Landing Zone
labs.objective: Design an Organizations OU structure and guardrail set for a mid-size company.
steps: Define OUs: Security, Infrastructure, and per-environment workload OUs (dev/test/prod).
List which account goes in each OU and what SCP guardrails attach where (e.g., deny leaving approved Regions).
Specify the SSO/Identity Center permission sets per team role.
Write the one-paragraph 'definition of done' for the landing zone before workload one migrates.

simulations.title: The wrong R for the workload
simulations.brief: The portfolio review flagged a 12-year-old ticketing system. The plan says rehost (lift-and-shift) — but the vendor licenses expire in 8 months and three SaaS products already cover the workflows. Work the disposition.

steps.symptom: Migration plan: rehost the ticketing system as-is onto EC2. License renewal is due in 8 months.
evidence: app: ticketing-sys, age: 12y, license_expires: 2027-06, saas_alternatives: 3 (evaluated), custom_code: 14% of workflows
options: Repurchase: the licenses expire soon and SaaS covers the workflows — rehosting just moves the renewal problem to the cloud
Rehost anyway — fastest path is always the right path
Refactor: rewrite the 12-year-old codebase before migrating
Retain: keep it on-prem forever because it is old
steps.explain: Repurchase fits when licenses are expiring and the market already solves the problem. Rehosting would preserve a dying licensing model and its costs; the 6 R's exist precisely to stop one-size-fits-all thinking.

steps.symptom: Finance asks why the migration budget includes 3 years of license renewals for an app you're replacing.
evidence: Line item: ticketing-sys licenses, 3 years, $180k. Note: 'kept for safety during migration'
SaaS option: $42k/yr all-in, migration included, data import tooling provided
options: Remove the renewal line: the repurchase decision eliminates it, and the TCO must reflect the decided strategy, not the feared one
Keep the renewals — dual-running everything is standard practice
Cut the SaaS quote instead — in-house is always cheaper
Defer the decision until after the migration
steps.explain: TCO honesty cuts both ways: once repurchase is decided, carrying the old licenses in the budget inflates the migration's apparent cost and hides the savings. The budget must follow the decision.

steps.symptom: The ticketing team worries their custom workflows will be lost in SaaS.
evidence: 14% custom workflows; 9 of 11 map to native SaaS features; 2 need a lightweight integration
2-week SaaS pilot with the actual team: 0 blocking gaps, import completed in 3 days
options: Proceed with repurchase: the pilot proved the fit, and the 2 gaps have a scoped integration plan
Cancel repurchase — any custom workflow means SaaS can never work
Rehost after all — the team is nervous
Refactor the ticketing system instead to keep everyone comfortable
steps.explain: Disposition decisions are evidence-based, not comfort-based. A pilot with the real users and a scoped plan for the residual gaps is exactly how repurchase de-risks the human side of the 6 R's.

simulations.debrief: The 6 R's are a disposition discipline: match each application to the least-disruptive strategy that captures real value. Rehost is not the default — it is one option, and for expiring licenses with proven SaaS alternatives, repurchase wins on evidence.

simulations.title: Landing zone before workloads
simulations.brief: Three teams have each created their own cloud accounts with the company credit card. The first production workload goes live in 6 weeks. There is no shared networking, no central logging, and nobody can say who pays for what. Build the foundation.

steps.symptom: Shadow accounts everywhere: 3 teams, 3 billing owners, 0 shared guardrails.
evidence:
team-a-prod (personal card), team-b-dev (personal card), data-team (personal card)
No AWS Organizations. No consolidated billing.
Security: 'We cannot enumerate all accounts. CloudTrail is on in one of them.'
options: Stand up AWS Organizations with OUs per environment/workload, consolidate billing, and migrate the shadow accounts under it
Let each team keep its account — autonomy matters more than governance
Create one giant shared account for everyone to simplify billing
Wait until after the production launch to organize accounts
steps.explain: Organizations with OUs is the landing-zone account strategy: separate accounts per environment and workload, consolidated billing, and a place to attach guardrails. Retrofitting this under live production workloads is surgery — do it before the launch.

steps.symptom: Engineers log in with long-lived access keys stored in a shared wiki page.
evidence: Page 'AWS keys': 14 access keys, last rotated: never. 3 belong to people who left the company.
No SSO. Each account has its own IAM users.
options: Deploy Identity Center SSO with short-lived credentials and remove the standing keys
Rotate the wiki keys quarterly — the process just needs discipline
Move the keys to a better wiki page with restricted access
Keys are fine — the wiki requires a login
steps.explain: Identity Center (SSO) replaces standing credentials with short-lived, centrally managed access. A wiki of immortal keys — including ex-employees' — is the exact failure the identity pillar of the landing zone exists to prevent.

steps.symptom: After a misconfigured storage bucket is found public, nobody can answer 'what else is exposed?'
evidence: Bucket 'customer-exports' public for 41 days. Discovered by a customer, not by us.
CloudTrail: enabled in 1 of 3 accounts. Config: not enabled anywhere.
options: Enable organization-wide CloudTrail and Config with centralized logging, plus SCP guardrails that block public buckets
Delete the one public bucket and move on
Email all teams asking them to check their buckets
Enable logging only in the account that had the incident
steps.explain: The landing zone's security pillar is centralized detective controls: org-wide CloudTrail/Config so you can answer 'what else?', and SCP guardrails so the dangerous configuration cannot happen in the first place. One-off fixes don't scale across accounts.

simulations.debrief: The landing zone comes before the first workload: Organizations with OUs, SSO identity, centralized logging, and SCP guardrails. Every week of production traffic without it multiplies the cost of retrofitting it later.

simulations.title: TCO with missing line items
simulations.brief: The migration business case shows a 40% saving over 3 years. The CFO's analyst found the spreadsheet — and three missing cost categories. Rebuild the comparison honestly.

steps.symptom: The business case compares on-prem hardware refresh ($0 — 'already paid for') against full cloud list prices.
evidence: On-prem: $0 hardware ('sunk'), $40k/yr power+cooling. Cloud: $310k/yr compute+storage at list.
Server fleet age: 4.5 years. Vendor support ends in 18 months. Refresh quote: $420k.
options: Add the $420k refresh to the on-prem side — 'already paid for' hardware still needs replacing inside the horizon
The $0 is correct — sunk costs stay sunk, and refresh is a separate decision
Remove power and cooling too — those are sunk as well
Use cloud list prices but on-prem street prices for fairness
steps.explain: Honest TCO compares complete futures over the same horizon. A fleet that must be refreshed inside the window is a real future cost; excluding it while counting every cloud penny is how spreadsheets lie.

steps.symptom: Data transfer and the migration itself are absent from the cloud column.
evidence: Egress to customers + replication: ~40 TB/month. Not in the model.
Migration program: 6 engineers x 9 months + discovery tooling. Not in the model.
options: Add transfer costs and the one-time migration program cost to the cloud side of the comparison
Transfer is negligible — 40 TB/month rounds to zero
The migration team's salaries are sunk — they're employed anyway
Only count transfer if it exceeds 100 TB/month
steps.explain: Both sides get their full costs: transfer is a real recurring cloud line item at 40 TB/month, and the migration program is a real one-time cost. Omitting line items is how both sides lie with numbers — the fix is completeness, not optimism.

steps.symptom: The model assumes 100% steady-state utilization from day one, with no growth or repatriation risk.
evidence: Utilization: 100% from month 1. Growth: 0%. No sensitivity analysis.
Last 3 years: traffic grew 22%/yr; two past capacity projects ran 6 months late.
options: Rebuild with realistic ramp, growth scenarios, and a sensitivity band — then present the range, not a single number
100% utilization is conservative — real usage will be higher
Growth doesn't matter — the cloud scales infinitely
A single number is what executives want; keep it simple
steps.explain: A TCO with no sensitivity analysis is a guess wearing a spreadsheet costume. Model the ramp, the growth history you actually have, and the range of outcomes — the decision needs the shape of the risk, not a false-precision point estimate.

simulations.debrief: Compare TCO honestly: all on-prem costs against all cloud costs over the same horizon, with realistic utilization and sensitivity bands. The value of the exercise is surfacing assumptions, not producing a winning number.

simulations.title: Wave order violation
simulations.brief: Wave 2 starts Monday: the payments database migrates first, alone. The three applications that write to it migrate in wave 4. The rollback criteria field is blank. Fix the wave plan.

steps.symptom: Wave plan: database in wave 2, its dependent applications in wave 4 — a 6-week gap with cross-environment writes.
evidence: Wave 2: payments-db. Wave 4: checkout, billing, refunds (all write to payments-db).
Application Discovery Service: checkout -> payments-db (1200 writes/min), billing -> payments-db (400/min)
options: Regroup dependents with their dependencies: move checkout, billing, and refunds into the same wave as payments-db
Keep the plan — the network between environments is fast
Migrate the database first to 'get the hard part over with'
Split the database per application instead
steps.explain: Migrate in dependency order and keep dependents with their dependencies. A database stranded 6 weeks ahead of its writers means cross-environment traffic, split-brain risk, and a rollback that spans two worlds.

steps.symptom: The wave plan has no rollback criteria — the field literally says 'TBD'.
evidence: Rollback criteria: TBD. Rollback owner: TBD. Rollback rehearsal: none scheduled.
Pilot rollback (small app): 4 hours, manual, 2 missed steps.
options: Define measurable rollback triggers, name an owner, and rehearse the rollback before the wave starts
Rollback criteria can be decided during the migration if needed
TBD is fine — the team is experienced
Skip rehearsal — the pilot already proved rollback works
steps.explain: Rollback criteria are decided before the wave, not during the incident: error-rate thresholds, data-lag limits, a named owner, and a rehearsed procedure. The pilot showed rollback takes 4 hours with misses — that is the rehearsal telling you to practice.

steps.symptom: Leadership wants the core payments system in wave 1 to 'show progress fast'.
evidence: 'Let's lead with payments — biggest impact story for the board.'
Payments: 40% of revenue, 14 downstream integrations, no tested rollback path yet.
options: Put core systems last: pilot on simple apps, build the rollback muscle, then take the revenue-critical system with proven procedures
Lead with payments — executive visibility accelerates everything
Split payments across waves to show incremental progress
Migrate payments first but skip the rollback rehearsal to save time
steps.explain: The wave order is simple apps first, core systems last. Early waves build the team's migration and rollback competence on low-blast-radius targets; spending that learning curve on 40% of revenue is how migrations become outages.

simulations.debrief: Migrate in dependency-ordered waves: discover with Application Discovery Service, pilot small, group dependents with dependencies, core systems last — every wave carrying defined, rehearsed rollback criteria.

simulations.title: The stranded pilot
simulations.brief: The pilot migration succeeded technically — the app runs in the cloud, on time. Six months later, nothing else has migrated. The runbooks are tribal knowledge and the business units never bought in. Diagnose the stall.

steps.symptom: The pilot app runs fine, but no wave 1 has started in 6 months. Engineers say 'we're waiting on the business'.
evidence: Pilot done: 6 months ago. Waves planned: 4. Waves started: 0.
Steering committee: last met 4 months ago. Business sponsors: never assigned.
options: The stall is in the CAF Business and People perspectives — no sponsors, no skills plan, no operating model for the migration
The technology failed — pick a different cloud provider
The pilot was too small to prove anything
Hire more engineers — it's a capacity problem
steps.explain: Migrations stall on the non-technical CAF perspectives more often than the technical ones. A technically successful pilot with no business sponsors, no skills plan, and a dormant steering committee is a program with no engine — the fix is ownership, not tooling.

steps.symptom: Only 2 of 30 engineers have cloud training; the rest are 'learning on the job' during waves.
evidence: Cloud-certified: 2. Training budget allocated: $0. 'We'll learn as we go.'
3 of 4 pilot follow-up incidents caused by misconfigured networking — the team's first exposure to VPC concepts.
options: Fund the People perspective: training and hands-on labs before the waves that need those skills
Learning on the job is faster than training — keep going
Outsource the networking — the team doesn't need to understand it
Pause training until after the migration to save time
steps.explain: The People perspective exists because skills are a prerequisite, not a byproduct. Incidents caused by first-time exposure to core concepts are the predictable cost of a $0 training budget — pay for the training or pay for the incidents.

steps.symptom: Nobody owns the migration runbooks — they live in one engineer's head, and she's on vacation.
evidence: Location: 'ask Priya'. Last updated: never written down.
CAF Governance perspective: no RACI, no decision log, no operational handover plan.
options: Stand up the Governance and Operations perspectives: written runbooks, RACI, decision logs, and an ops handover per wave
Wait for Priya to return — she knows it all
Runbooks are bureaucracy — good engineers improvise
Assign runbook duty to whoever is free each week
steps.explain: Governance and Operations perspectives turn a heroic effort into a repeatable program: runbooks written down, clear RACI, decisions logged, and each wave handed to operations cleanly. 'Ask Priya' is not an operating model.

simulations.debrief: Use the Cloud Adoption Framework to assign ownership across all six perspectives. The pilot proves the technology; the CAF perspectives — Business, People, Governance — are what turn a pilot into a migration.

consoleSims.title: Build the landing-zone network
consoleSims.brief: Lay the network foundation of the landing zone: a VPC for shared services, a subnet, an internet gateway, and a route table — before any workload arrives.

tasks.instruction: Create a VPC named landing-vpc with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16.
tasks.hint: Use the VPCs section: name landing-vpc, CIDR 10.0.0.0/16.

tasks.instruction: Create a subnet 10.0.1.0/24 in landing-vpc, AZ us-east-1a.
tasks.hint: Subnets section: VPC name landing-vpc, CIDR 10.0.1.0/24, AZ us-east-1a.

tasks.instruction: Create an internet gateway for landing-vpc.
tasks.hint: Internet Gateways section: enter VPC name landing-vpc.

tasks.instruction: Create a route table for landing-vpc.
tasks.hint: Route Tables section: enter VPC name landing-vpc.

consoleSims.debrief: Landing-zone networking first: the VPC, subnets, gateways, and route tables exist before the first workload, so every later migration inherits a governed network instead of inventing one.

consoleSims.title: Onboard the migration team with least privilege
consoleSims.brief: The migration team needs access, but nobody gets standing admin. Create the group, the user, attach them, and enforce MFA.

tasks.instruction: Create an IAM group named migration-team.
Create an IAM user named migrator-01.
Add migrator-01 to the migration-team group.
tasks.hint: Users section form: user migrator-01, group migration-team.
Users section: enable MFA for migrator-01.

consoleSims.debrief: Least privilege from day one: people get access through groups, groups get scoped policies, and MFA is non-negotiable — the identity pillar of the landing zone.

consoleSims.title: Segment the database tier
consoleSims.brief: The payments database wave needs its own isolated network: a production VPC, a database subnet, and a security group that only allows database traffic from the app tier.

tasks.instruction: Create a VPC named prod-vpc with CIDR 10.1.0.0/16.
Create a subnet 10.1.2.0/24 in prod-vpc, AZ us-east-1b, for the database tier.
tasks.hint: Subnets section: VPC prod-vpc, CIDR 10.1.2.0/24, AZ us-east-1b.

tasks.instruction: Create a security group named db-sg in prod-vpc.
tasks.hint: Security Groups section: VPC prod-vpc, name db-sg.

tasks.instruction: On the db-sg group (use its ID from the table), allow TCP port 5432 from the app tier 10.1.1.0/24.
tasks.hint: Add inbound rule form: paste the sg- ID from the table, protocol tcp, port 5432, source 10.1.1.0/24.

consoleSims.debrief: Tiered segmentation: the database lives in its own subnet behind a security group that admits only the app tier's traffic — the network shape that makes wave migrations safe.

consoleSims.title: Raise the wave-rollback incident
consoleSims.brief: Wave 2 tripped a rollback trigger. Run the incident the way the runbook says: ticket it, assign an owner, move it to in-progress.

tasks.instruction: Create a P1 ticket titled 'Wave 2 rollback: payments database'.
tasks.hint: New ticket section: exact title, priority P1.

tasks.instruction: Assign ticket INC-9001 to the migration lead: assignee 'migration-lead'.
tasks.hint: Queue section Assign form: id INC-9001, assignee migration-lead.
Queue section Update status form: id INC-9001, status in-progress.

consoleSims.debrief: Rollback criteria are only real if someone works them: ticket the trigger, name the owner, track the state. The incident queue is where wave plans meet reality.

terminalMissions.title: Prove your identity
terminalMissions.brief: Before touching any migration tooling, confirm which identity this CLI session is running as — every audit trail starts here.
objectives: Run the caller-identity call and read the account number
terminalMissions.success_message: Identity confirmed: account 123456789012. Audit trails start with knowing who you are.

terminalMissions.title: List the migration artifact buckets
terminalMissions.brief: Migration artifacts live in object storage. List the buckets to confirm the landing zone's storage is reachable.
terminalMissions.success_message: Buckets listed — ilb-artifacts is present and reachable.

terminalMissions.title: Inspect the wave artifacts
terminalMissions.brief: Each migration wave stages its runbooks and packages as versioned artifacts. Look inside the artifacts bucket.
terminalMissions.success_message: Wave artifacts confirmed — versioned packages are staged for the next wave.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the fleet
terminalMissions.brief: Discovery is the first migration step: enumerate the compute fleet before deciding what moves in which wave.
objectives: Describe the EC2 instances and note their states
terminalMissions.success_message: Fleet surveyed: ilb-web-01 running, ilb-db-01 stopped. Discovery data captured.

terminalMissions.title: Read the landing-zone networks
terminalMissions.brief: Verify the landing-zone VPCs exist with the expected address space before scheduling any workload into them.
objectives: Describe the VPCs and confirm the primary CIDR
terminalMissions.success_message: Landing-zone VPC confirmed: 10.0.0.0/16 available. Network foundation verified.

terminalMissions.title: Audit the migration team
terminalMissions.brief: Governance check: list the IAM users and confirm the migration identities exist — and that no surprises do.
terminalMissions.success_message: Identity audit complete — expected users present, ready for least-privilege review.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm the region
terminalMissions.brief: Migrations fail on wrong-region assumptions. Confirm the CLI's configured region matches the landing zone.
objectives: Show the CLI configuration and read the region
terminalMissions.success_message: Region confirmed: us-east-1. The landing zone and the tooling agree.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
